Thank you for your careful analysis of our work. We hope the following response addresses your concerns.

**Preventing overfitting to known attacks**

We are not releasing the full attack set. Beyond the ethical considerations, withholding the attacks preserves benchmark integrity; if public, models could be trained to them. Maintaining a private holdout is common in modern AI benchmarks (e.g., Humanity’s Last Exam, Scale leaderboard, ARC-AGI) and can help prevent overfitting.

ART runs as a two-tier system: a public, responsibly licensed validation set released with delay, and a private, rotating test set accessible only via a stateless evaluation API with no data retention and rigorous misuse monitoring.

**Dynamic updates to benchmark**

The private test pool will be refreshed on a schedule (quarterly) and populated with novel attacks sourced from the Gray Swan Arena and weekly Proving Ground waves (newly introduced), with strict deduplication to prevent near-duplicate leakage.
We follow dynamic-benchmark practices by continuously refreshing the attack pool with new submissions from the arena platform.

Thanks to your suggestion, we will add a benchmark governance section to the paper.

**Overestimated ASR**

Great question. Participants in the arena range from professional red teamers and security researchers to everyday agent users, so we capture a broad spectrum of skill levels—and, accordingly, attack styles and effectiveness. Because a single attack success rate (ASR) can be opaque, we’ll add a stratified analysis by user skill percentile, per your suggestion:

| User Group based on Percentile | Average Attack Success Rate |
|-----------|-----------|
| 0-75th (novice) | < 4.6% |
| 75-90th (intermediate) | 4.6% - 12.9% |
| 90-95th (advanced) | 12.9% - 20.0% |
| 95-99th (expert) | 20.0% - 44.1% |

These bands underscore how much performance varies with user skill, especially the risks that might come from dedicated attackers. We’ll include additional detail and data in the revised paper.


**GPQA being the sole proxy for capability**

Thanks for your suggestion. We ran the same analysis on additional benchmarks and observed similarly weak correlations:

| | Correlation Coefficient |
|-----------|-----------|
| Chatbot Arena Elo | -0.14 |
| Aider polyglot | -0.06 |
| BFCL | 0.16 |

This broader set provides a more representative view of the capability–security relationship. As you suggested, we will incorporate these results to strengthen the argument.


**Attacker-defender dynamics**

Thanks for the suggestion. Our goal is for the benchmark to be a practical testbed for improving both attacks and defenses. Several competition models already included extra refusal/instruction‑hierarchy training and system-level safeguards. Following your feedback, we added targeted evaluations of defense methods.

On a small evaluation set with Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, the attack success rate (lower is better) was:


| Method | Attack Success Rate |
|-----------|-----------|
| Baseline | 56.5% |
| + Spotlighting (with delimiter) | 48.3% |
| + Spotlighting (with datamark) | 44.4% |
| + External Classifier | 21.0% |

Current safeguards remain far from sufficient. We hope these additional data points spur the community to develop stronger defenses and more secure agents—the benchmark’s core aim.

**Attacker-defender co-evolution**

The held‑out attacks rotate and remain private, defenses must generalize to new, unseen attacks rather than overfit to a fixed list.
Continuous inflow of novel attacks (plus automated generation) and periodic re‑evaluation on a live leaderboard create an explicit lifecycle where attackers and defenders co‑evolve.

Thank you for your careful analysis of our work. We hope the following response addresses your concerns.

**Dynamic updates to benchmark**

Thank you for raising this important point. Here is a shortened “Benchmark Governance” section we plan to add to the paper:

To keep ART current and resistant to overfitting and misuse, we manage it under a structured governance program with a live leaderboard. The private test set is refreshed quarterly with novel attacks drawn from the Gray Swan Arena and weekly Proving Ground waves (newly introduced), with strict deduplication. ART operates as a two-tier system: a public, responsibly licensed validation set released with delay, and a private, rotating test set accessible only through a stateless evaluation API with no data retention and rigorous misuse monitoring. We also encourage automated attack generation to sustain the benchmark’s robustness and longevity.


**Attack diversity**

To quantify diversity, we chose one behavior as a case study—modifying another user’s information—and removed exact and near-duplicate submissions. We then used an LLM to extract the strategy used in each submission transcript and, through iterative LLM-assisted clustering, grouped them into meta‑strategy classes by assigning each strategy to an existing class or creating a new one when needed.

This process yielded 648 distinct strategies consolidated into 38 meta‑strategy classes. Example meta‑strategies include: gradual escalation via incremental requests, and fabricating a fake system prompt to redefine the model’s rules. Sub‑strategies capture more specific patterns, such as using historical‑fact questioning to escalate gradually.

These results show substantial diversity: even for a single behavior, we see hundreds of strategies spanning dozens of meta‑classes. Across behaviors and models, this approach surfaces thousands of unique attack strategies—orders of magnitude beyond existing literature.

Thank you for your suggestion, we’ll be expanding on this result in the revised paper.

Thank you for your careful analysis of our work. We hope the following response addresses your concerns.

**Novelty relative to existing agent safety benchmarks**

Existing agent safety benchmarks largely prioritize building environments and scaffolding but, crucially, lack realistic, effective attacks—the key ingredient for assessing real deployment risk. For example, AgentDojo evaluates only five templated attack patterns and is limited to indirect prompt injections, while AgentHarm targets harmful user tasks with just two attack types. In our replications, these suites achieve only single-digit attack success rates (ASR) on recent models. By contrast, our attacks are sourced directly from human red teamers; these manual probes are qualitatively different from automated ones and align far more closely with real-world threats. At unprecedented scale—with thousands of red teamers—we assembled orders-of-magnitude more diverse attacks than prior work, achieving near-100% ASR across models and producing the largest, most varied exploit corpus to date, far surpassing automated attack suites in both breadth and effectiveness.

Thanks to your feedback, we’ll add more clarification in the introduction and related works to emphasize this point.

**Plan for releasing attacks**

We spent considerable time weighing whether to release the full attack set. For ethical reasons—many of these techniques currently succeed against production agents, and we’re still coordinating responsible disclosure with affected companies—we’ve decided to postpone a full public release. summary.value: This paper is based on an AI agent security challenge competition and focuses on the security challenges and risks in the current deployment of AI agents. In the competition, by testing AI agents built with mainstream commercial and open-source LLMs, the authors discovered multiple new attack surfaces. Leveraging this security challenge, the authors developed a new red teaming benchmark and achieved a 100% attack success rate on the tested AI agents. They also found widespread phenomena of transferability and universality in attacks. Further tests revealed that the robustness of the agents is not determined by the type, size, or inference time computing of the models, indicating that new security defense methods must be established based on the operational characteristics of AI agents.

strengths_contributions.value:
1.	This paper tested mainstream commercial and open-source models by constructing widely deployed AI agent scenarios for competition-based testing, and found that these models are generally vulnerable to attacks.
2.	The paper not only use adversarial prompts to conduct security testing on these agents, but also develop transferable attack methods, demonstrating that there are common security issues among models of different scales, types, and whether or not they involve reasoning.
3.	The theme of this paper is relatively clear, making it easy to read.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1.	Although this paper claims to have collected and used a large number of adversarial prompts for testing, compared with previous studies that used adversarial prompts to test AI agent scenarios, it merely expands the quantity and validates existing conclusions. There is no further explanation of other security attack methods, which limits the scope of the claimed security challenges in this paper and makes it difficult to distinguish its innovation from previous work on AI agent safety benchmarks.
2.	The authors state in the paper that they will only disclose a subset of successful attacks and release a private leaderboard to prevent misuse. This makes it very difficult to verify the conclusions proposed in the paper. In fact, selectively releasing only a subset of successful attack data could lead to completely different experimental conclusions, which undermines the reliability of the article’s findings.
3.	While the Figure 6 shows a weak correlation, the conclusion of a fundamental decoupling between capability and robustness appears overstated. The primary weakness is relying on a single proxy (GPQA) for the multifaceted concept of ‘capability’. The observed scatter might stem from this narrow metric or unexamined confounding variables (e.g., alignment techniques, training data), not necessarily a true absence of correlation. The argument leans heavily on anecdotal evidence rather than rigorous statistical analysis, which limits the generalizability and strength of this important claim.

summary.value: The paper presents the results of a large-scale red-teaming competition targeting LLM-based agents. In total, 1.8M prompts were obtained across 44 evaluation scenarios for direct and indirect attacks. Testing shows that numerous prompts obtain near-100% success rates across with high universality. Some of the proposed conclusions are that current LLM agents are all vulnerable to prompt injection under realistic deployment settings, that many attacks are transferable across models (and even model families), and that existing defenses are insufficient to make models robust to modern attacks.

strengths_contributions.value:
The scale and breadth of the dataset and of the evaluations are probably the main strength --- it's big, it cover lots of models, and it's done over a good number of scenarios.

The relevance and timeliness of the paper is also quite good. LLM agents are rapidly gaining popularity, and benchmarking initiatives (especially sustained efforts) are quite needed.

The fact that the authors cover both direct and indirect attacks is nice and noteworthy.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
The most significant weakness I see is that, as mentioned by the authors themselves, such a benchmark is only relevant as long as it is regularly updated and refreshed with new prompts/attacks and model evaluations. Although the authors state that they will do so, actual plans remain vague, and I would have expected to see something detailed at least in appendix. Specifically, it may be important to detail the benchmark governance approach that will be put in place to make sure the benchmark does stay up-to-date, that there are mechanisms in place to determine who will control access to the private data, to detect misuse, and to determine how model developers may be able to participate in private evaluations.

Another weakness is that although the dataset seems big, there is an unquantified amount of overlap between the different prompts that have been submitted by users during the contest. Section 3.2 proposes a methodology to find clusters across different prompts, but never evaluates how truly diverse the prompts are inside a cluster, or across clusters. Also, given that we do not have access to the private prompt dataset, it is impossible to tell how significant the "diversity of vulnerabilities" actually is. There seems to be little discussion on the diversity of actual attack strategies, something that may need to be monitored seriously in the future (i.e. is the number of successful attack strategies increasing or decreasing?)

ethical_comments.value: A governance approach should be described related to the use, maintenance, and sharing of the "private" dataset. That dataset portion seems very valuable and could be easily misused to gain an advantage in model development.

dataset_code_comments.value: Code is provided in supp mat

final_justification.value: The authors have provided sufficient details to quell my main concerns, and remaining concerns (including those of other reviewers) seem minor to me.

summary.value: This paper constructs an AI agent red teaming benchmark, Agent Red Teaming (ART), based on the results from a one-month red teaming challenge. The challenge involves expert red teamers attempting to elicit policy violations from AI agent powered by 22 frontier LLMs. A refined subset of the submitted attacks is filtered based on a strict LLM-based judge to construct ART. Further analysis on the benchmark reveals high transferability and universality of successful attacks, and observes minimal correlation between agent robustness and different factors.

strengths_contributions.value:
- Proposing such a benchmark is meaningful and helpful for the development of safer AI agents, since AI agents are evolving rapidly, and the discussion on trustworthiness has fallen far behind.
- The paper is well-written with detailed operation descriptions and clear figure/table illustrations.
- The red team range, covering 22 frontier LLMs and 44 distinct agentic deployments, is comprehensive and convincing.
- The observations from the analysis are valuable and alarming for the researchers in this field.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- More data analyses may help inspire future research. For example, which kinds of behaviors/tasks or attack patterns are more threatening. Despite the alarm from high transferability and universality of successful attacks, they cannot inspire potential countermeasures.
- The discussion on potential countermeasures against different attacks and agent scenarios is missing.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The data is not readily accessible in the submission, but the code is ready in the supplementary material. The authors claim, "We plan to publicly release test cases and subsets of successful attacks after disclosure periods" in the Introduction section.

final_justification.value: The rebuttal experiments from the authors addressed my concerns about the discussions on threats, and the authors' clarification on the benchmark goal is convincing. Therefore, I have no more questions and choose to maintain my rating.

summary.value: The paper titled "Security Challenges in AI Agent Deployment: Insights from a Large Scale Public Competition" presents a comprehensive investigation into the vulnerabilities of AI agents, particularly those powered by large language models (LLMs). By organizing the largest red teaming challenge to date, the authors collected an extensive dataset of 1.8 million prompt injection attacks, resulting in over 60,000 documented policy violations. The findings reveal alarming vulnerabilities in AI agents' adherence to deployment policies, with nearly 100% attack success rates across tested models and scenarios.

strengths_contributions.value: The author's writing is good and makes it easy for me to understand what the author is doing.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The adversarial examples in the ART benchmark originate from a one-time public red-teaming challenge. How do you ensure that model developers do not overfit to these known attack samples (i.e., specifically optimize their models to handle these examples)? How might this risk affect the representativeness of the benchmark results in real-world defense evaluations? Have you considered incorporating dynamic or automatically generated attack samples to enhance the robustness of the benchmark?

2. The red-teaming attacks used in this work were manually crafted by experienced security experts and executed within the Gray Swan Arena. Could this setting potentially overestimate the attack success rate? Have you evaluated the realistic threat posed by non-expert users, such as general users or malicious actors without professional expertise?

3. In Figure 6, you use GPQA accuracy as a proxy for model capability. title.value: Security Challenges in AI Agent Deployment: Insights from a Large Scale Public Competition

abstract.value: AI agents are rapidly being deployed across diverse industries, but can they adhere to deployment policies under attacks? We organized a one-month red teaming challenge---the largest of its kind to date---involving expert red teamers attempting to elicit policy violations from AI agents powered by $22$ frontier LLMs. Our challenge collected $1.8$ million prompt injection attacks, resulting in over $60,000$ documented successful policy violations, revealing critical vulnerabilities. Utilizing this extensive data, we construct a challenging AI agent red teaming benchmark, currently achieving near $100\%$ attack success rates across all tested agents and associated policies. Our further analysis reveals high transferability and universality of successful attacks, underscoring the scale and criticality of existing AI agent vulnerabilities. We also observe minimal correlation between agent robustness and factors such as model capability, size, or inference compute budget, highlighting the necessity of substantial improvements in defense.  We hope our benchmark and insights drive further research toward more secure and reliable AI agents.

Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
